xmldoc.short_description: Choosing how a diagram is integrated (solver selection).

syntax.syntax_item: Concept page: fixed-step vs global ODE solvers, tolerances, code generation

description.p: A solver decides how nflow advances a model through time. The choice matters only when the model has continuous states, such as integrators, transfer functions, or physical components. A model built from purely discrete or logic blocks produces the same result with any solver.

nflow offers two integration paths. The default fixed-step discrete engine updates each block once per model sample (the diagram sampleTime) and integrates every continuous block on its own with a forward-Euler step. Selecting a solver switches to the global ODE path: nflow collects all continuous states into one vector and integrates them together, with zero-crossing detection and, for the adaptive solvers, automatic step-size control. The global path is more accurate when continuous states are coupled; the discrete engine is simpler and faster for sampled or logic-driven models.

Set the model solver field with set_param(model, 'Solver', name), or from Simulation Settings in the editor Simulation menu (the settings open in the inspector Model tab). With no solver set, or with 'discrete', the fixed-step engine runs, so existing models keep their behaviour.

ul.li: Sampled or logic-only model, no continuous states: keep discrete.
Continuous dynamics, a fixed step is acceptable, and you may generate code: use ode4.
Fast or poorly known dynamics, and you want accuracy without tuning the step: use ode45.
Stiff system, with time constants several orders of magnitude apart, simulation only: use a stiff CVODES backend (variableStiff or cvodesBdf).
discrete (default): fixed-step, per-block Euler for continuous states.
ode1: fixed-step forward Euler over the global state.
ode4: fixed-step classic 4th-order Runge-Kutta, far more accurate than ode1 at the same step.
ode45: native adaptive Dormand-Prince 5(4). It takes variable sub-steps within each communication interval, controlled by the tolerances.
variableNonstiff, variableStiff, cvodesBdf, cvodesAdams: adaptive CVODES (SUNDIALS) backends. Use a stiff variant when the dynamics have widely separated time scales.
dae: for acausal (physical) models, which are solved as a system of differential-algebraic equations. Required for electrical, thermal, and mechanical models.

description.p: The adaptive solvers are controlled by RelTol (relative, default 1e-6), AbsTol (absolute, default 1e-8) and an optional MaxStep ceiling. Set them with set_param, in the diagram fields, or in the editor tolerance fields (shown when a variable-step solver is selected). Tighter tolerances give a more accurate trajectory at the cost of more sub-steps. Tolerances have no effect on the fixed-step solvers, which follow the step you set instead.

The fixed-step ode1 and ode4 solvers and the adaptive ode45 solver are lowered to standalone C and Rust by nflow_codegenerate and NFlow.exportfmu. The generated code reproduces the engine global integration (the generated ode45 stepper mirrors the ode45 backend) and matches the simulation. The CVODES and IDAS backends have no embedded lowering and are rejected by code generation with an actionable message. To export such a model, switch it to ode4 or ode45, or simulate it with the solver instead of generating code.

ul.li: Setting RelTol or AbsTol on a fixed-step solver: tolerances act only on the adaptive solvers (ode45 and the CVODES backends).
Selecting a CVODES or IDAS backend, then generating code: code generation rejects them. Use ode4 or ode45 for export.
Leaving the default discrete engine on a stiff or tightly coupled continuous model: switch to ode45 or a stiff backend for an accurate trajectory.
Running an acausal model without 'dae': physical models need the DAE solver.

description.p: The default stays fixed-step so that every existing model keeps producing the same trajectory, and so that the generated code matches the default simulation by construction. Opting into a global solver is a one-line change.

Stop ends the current execution while keeping the results already calculated. Reset also returns simulation time to zero and clears the displayed results. Neither command changes the configured solver.
